description: We are Second Toe, a team of five. We are building a handheld fire-safety console for spacecraft crew. It uses NASA microgravity combustion data to estimate whether a flame keeps burning, and it warns when settings fall outside what experiments tested. We work in Python and web (HTML/JS), with an PC for modeling and a Lenovo Legion Go as the handheld. Our team is complete.
summary:
Could a future Moon crew use NASA’s combustion data to choose a solid cabin panel? Flame in Freefall lets users investigate that question. The dashboard ranks 24 NASA investigations by their relevance to fire prevention, detection, suppression or cabin atmosphere. Its Oxygen map compares nine experimental tables. Of 746 published rows with ambient oxygen and pressure, 20 meet the challenge’s Moon Base thresholds. All 20 describe gas flames. Users can inspect each source row and see why the behavior of a solid panel in lunar gravity remains an open question.

The Flame console lets users change fuel and cabin conditions, compare model estimates with recorded droplet tests, and see when nearby experiments gave inconclusive results. The core activities work offline and support handheld controls. An optional local assistant, Ember, answers questions using NASA records. Together, these tools help students, engineers and mission planners decide which findings apply to their question and what still needs testing.
details:
Flame in Freefall helps students, engineers and mission planners find the NASA experiments most relevant to a spacecraft fire-safety question. The dashboard opens in Orbit view, where 24 investigations from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository are arranged by relevance. Choose Detection and the SAME smoke experiments move toward the center. Switch to Cabin air and the ACME Burning Rate Emulator takes the lead. Each investigation explains what researchers measured, why it matters and where to find the original record.

Crew mode turns the Flame console into a handheld briefing. It shows the selected cabin conditions and the limits of the available evidence before presenting a prediction. Users can open the controls to change a setting, inspect nearby NASA tests on the star map, and return to the full console with the same inputs. We chose physical controls so users can keep their eyes on the evidence. For example, they can sweep the stick to vary oxygen, watch the reading change and feel a vibration when the setting leaves the tested range. We considered how controls that can be located by feel might help someone wearing gloves. We tested the stick, buttons, touchscreen and vibration on a Lenovo Legion Go. Gloved use and in-flight operation remain untested.

The Moon evidence check asks whether existing experiments could help a crew choose a solid panel for a lunar cabin. The Oxygen map compares nine tables from seven investigations. Of 746 published rows with ambient oxygen and pressure, 20 meet the challenge thresholds of at least 30% oxygen and at most 10.2 psi. Users can inspect the fuel, conditions and original CSV line for every match. All 20 describe gas flames. The activity leaves users with a precise question for a future experiment: how would the panel itself burn under lunar gravity?

The Flame console lets users save a baseline, change conditions and compare predictions with results from NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX). At the default heptane settings for the Moon Base preset, the model displays a 99% chance of burning to completion among tests with a clear outcome. A separate model estimates a 98% chance of disruption at those same settings. All three nearby experiments were recorded as disruptions. Seeing the recorded outcomes alongside both estimates helps users understand how little direct evidence supports a conclusion about completion.

We built the dashboard with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, prepared the NASA tables with Python and pandas, and trained three models with scikit-learn. The completion model uses 199 clear FLEX outcomes. The disruption and burning-rate models use all 252 in-scope rows. A downloaded copy works offline, including activities that compare Earth and orbital burn lengths, reveal gas sensor measurements and show six NASA experiment clips. With a local Ollama server, users can also ask Ember about the research. For BASS-II gas questions, Python checks Ember’s proposed filter and returns the matching NASA rows so users can verify the measurements themselves.

Source code and documentation: https://github.com/jeerun/flame-in-freefall

Watch the full walkthrough: https://youtu.be/LwbnjOe0VXI

Watch our team use the physical controls on a Lenovo Legion Go to play Fire Drill in this 28-second hands-on demo: https://youtu.be/h12GSeM07Yw
